kf1.tip: Predict what happens to the primacy effect and the recency effect if people do a distracting task before recall, then explain each using STM and LTM.
kf1.note: The recency effect disappears and the primacy effect remains. The last few words were only held in short-term memory, so the distracting task lets that STM trace fade before recall. The first few words got the most rehearsal, so they were transferred to long-term memory, where they stay safe. If you said both effects vanish, check your reasoning. LTM traces persist while STM traces fade quickly.

kf2.tip: Change Murdock's method so participants do a distracting task before recalling the 20 words. Say what happens to primacy and recency, and why.
kf2.note: A strong answer weighs which store each end of the list is recalled from, what the distraction does to STM, and what stays in LTM. Most would conclude that recency disappears while primacy remains, so the curve loses its right-hand rise. This is what the multi-store model predicts. The trap is saying all recall drops evenly, or not explaining why early words survive: rehearsal moved them into LTM.

cs1.tip: Sketch the serial position curve from memory, label both axes, primacy and recency, and note beside each end which store those words are recalled from.
cs1.note: A good sketch puts probability of recall on the vertical axis and position in the list on the horizontal axis. The line must be U-shaped. It starts high for the first few words, dips in the middle, then rises again for the last few. Label the left rise primacy and note it is recalled from LTM. Label the right rise recency and note it is recalled from STM. If you swapped the stores, remember that the early words were rehearsed into LTM.
